newsitem.title: BELARUS: Everyone votes "Yes' in new Belarus parliament.
newsitem.headline: Everyone votes "Yes' in new Belarus parliament.

text.p: President Alexander Lukashenko's new parliament met in the former Komsomol headquarters in Belarus on Tuesday and deputies raised their hands in a display of Soviet-style unanimity to support him.
About 110 deputies attended the alternative session in what was once the headqarters of the Communist youth league, just 100 metres (yards) from the president's administration.
Lukashenko, escorted by a bodyguard protecting him from thick snow with an umbrella, walked across the road from his office to tend his parliamentary flock.

It was a far cry from the old parliament, split down the middle between supporters and opponents of Lukashenko. Here, everybody backed the 42-year-old head of state, who several times interrupted deputies' speeches to make comments.
The president, who won a controversial referendum on Sunday to extend his powers, sat sipping tea as deputies passed new laws to formalise his dream of staying in power beyond 2000.
Deputies showed unanimous support for the tall, angular, moustachioed leader 13 times, with no abstentions. Only two proposals, on minor one-word amendments, attracted resistance.
They made the referendum legally binding, in line with one of Lukashenko's decrees which was opposed by the old parliament and the constitutional court.
Lukashenko told them that by giving the referendum legal force they had "done no less for the country than the president who initiated the referendum".
Deputies also told the constitutional court to drop impeachment proceedings against Lukashenko begun by opposition deputies last week. The court later followed instructions and dropped the case.
"The Constitutional Court still plays games. But you will stop it. You must do that!" Lukashenko told deputies.
"The Supreme Soviet cannot give recommendations to the president," Lukashenko declared -- and his parliament's new speaker hastened to concur.
"I absolutely agree with the opinion expressed just there," responded Yuri Malumov, deputy speaker of the old parliament who has defected to chair the new one.

Everyone spoke Russian, like Lukashenko, and all the documents were printed in Russian, while at the old parliament several dozen deputies spoke Belarussian. Both languages are used officially in the country between Poland and Russia.
But the victorious president also promised not to put any pressure on those deputies who had remained in the old parliament rather than joining his team.
"If they want to work -- please join the session. Noone should be forced, pressured, the people should have a right to correct their mistakes and to have their own opinion," he said.
But he made clear he had the power to make life better for those who crossed to his side.

When some deputies complained that they had "material" problems they were immediately calmed by Lukashenko's words: "Comrades! I'll help you...If you need communication, passes, money and means -- everything goes through the Finance Ministry. I'll get everything for you!"
